planting.note: Set out a grafted tree in a warm, wind-sheltered spot once frost danger has fully passed and soil has warmed; Pace is a cross of the 'Magana' and 'Tazumal' mamey sapotes and runs more cold-tolerant than most other named selections.

directions: Pace bears precociously and heavily on a somewhat smaller, more manageable tree than many older mamey sapote selections. Fruit runs on the small side for the species, with sweet orange-red flesh, and ripens in an early-spring window when few other fresh tree fruits are available on the Gulf Coast. Young trees are still frost-tender and benefit from wind shelter and trunk wraps their first several winters, though established trees tolerate brief dips into the low 30s better than most other named cultivars. Harvest fruit while still firm and let it finish softening at room temperature indoors.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden Plant Records
Morton, J. Fruits of Warm Climates

planting.note: Set out a grafted tree in a warm, wind-sheltered spot once frost danger has fully passed and soil has warmed thoroughly.

directions: Tazumal traces to a seedling tree brought to Homestead, Florida from El Salvador in 1949 and remains prized for fast growth and heavy annual bearing, often producing a light second flush in summer alongside its main winter-to-spring crop. Fruit is medium-sized with rich pink flesh of excellent flavor, carrying a few more seeds than some competing selections. Grow it as you would other mamey sapote: deep, well-drained soil, full sun, and room for a large long-term canopy, expecting several years to first fruiting even from a grafted tree. Its vigor makes Tazumal a useful pollinizer companion planted alongside a primary eating cultivar.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden Plant Records
HortTechnology — mamey sapote cultivar trials, Puerto Rico

planting.note: Set out a grafted tree in a warm, wind-sheltered spot once frost danger has fully passed and soil has warmed thoroughly.

directions: Copan is a Cuban-origin selection producing medium fruit with deep red flesh of outstanding quality and typically only one large seed, making it easier to prepare than seedier cultivars. It bears more lightly than heavy producers like 'Pantin' or 'Magana', so it suits a home dessert planting rather than a commercial block. Culture matches other named mamey sapote selections: deep, fertile, well-drained soil, full sun, and generous space for a tall, long-lived tree that needs several years after planting before its first crop. Protect young trees from frost and wind, and harvest fruit firm, ripening it indoors at room temperature.
sources: HortTechnology — mamey sapote cultivar trials, Puerto Rico
University of Florida IFAS Extension
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden Plant Records

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after frost danger passes; in zone 9b-10 plant March-June with winter protection while young, since Bernicker is best suited to zones 10-11.

directions: Bernicker is a widely grown grafted selection prized for near-spherical, medium-to-large fruit that carries only one or two seeds, easier to eat and process than seedy seedling trees. It bears heavily and reliably, with fruit maturing over an extended fall-into-winter window, later than most other Gulf Coast tree fruits. Grow it in full sun to light shade in well-drained fertile soil, with patience, since the glossy evergreen tree needs several years to bear after planting. Pick fruit firm and green and let it fully soften at room temperature for a week or more before spooning out the dark, custard-textured flesh.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Black Sapote in the Home Landscape
California Rare Fruit Growers — Black Sapote Fruit Facts
Daleys Fruit Tree Nursery cultivar notes

common_name: Norris Che (Seedless Female Mandarin Melon Berry)

planting.note: Plant a grafted or rooted-cutting tree in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; like other che selections, Norris tolerates poor, dry, or alkaline soils far better than most fruiting trees.

directions: Norris was discovered growing near Norris Dam in Tennessee and, like 'Darrow', is a female che selection that sets a heavy, fully seedless crop without needing a male pollinator nearby. The maroon-red, bumpy-skinned fruits run one to two inches across and ripen to a sweet flavor often likened to a fig with a hint of watermelon. Grow it as you would 'Darrow': full sun, unfussy well-drained soil, and room for a thorny-when-young large shrub or small tree that responds well to formative pruning for easier harvest. Planting Norris alongside 'Darrow' or a male che is unnecessary for fruiting but can extend the ripening season.
sources: Cricket Hill Garden cultivar notes
North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
Edible Landscaping

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 4 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 plant March-June. Like other roselle, Victor is a short-day plant that sets flowers as late-summer days shorten, with calyx harvest running from late summer until frost.

directions: Victor is one of the oldest named roselle selections grown in the United States, introduced in Florida in the early twentieth century and still favored by south Florida home gardeners for large, bright-red, exceptionally plump calyces. The tall, vigorous plants yield a heavier calyx crop per bush than many seed-strain roselles sold today, and the reddish stems and lobed foliage make an attractive hedge-like screen through the season. Grow it in full sun, fertile well-drained soil, and generous spacing, harvesting calyces about a week after the petals drop while still firm and before the inner seed pod toughens. Use the tart calyces fresh or dried for tea, syrup, and jelly.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Roselle (Hibiscus sabdariffa)
ECHO Community — Roselle Production Notes
PFAF Plant Database

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or grafted plants in spring after frost danger passes; in zone 9 plant March-May. Cutting-grown Manoa Sweet plants can flower and fruit within their first year under warm conditions.

directions: Manoa Sweet was bred at the University of Hawaii and released in 1963 as a low-acid, mild-flavored acerola suited to eating fresh rather than only juicing, unlike sharply tart seedling Barbados cherries. The upright, spreading shrub is very productive, bearing repeated flushes of orange-red fruit through the warm season, and it reaches a larger mature size than compact selections like 'B-17', so give it more room in the landscape. Grow in full sun and well-drained fertile soil; the shrub takes light pruning well and can be shaped into a dense hedge or specimen. Fruit is thin-skinned, juicy, and highly perishable once ripe, so harvest and refrigerate or process it within a day or two.
sources: University of Hawaii CTAHR cultivar release records
California Rare Fruit Growers — Acerola Fruit Facts
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Acerola in the Home Landscape

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant March-May. Like 'Sabara', young Paulista trees need frost protection below 28F, while trees five years and older tolerate brief drops into the mid-20s.

directions: Paulista is one of the two most widely grown jaboticaba selections in Brazil alongside 'Sabara', distinguished by noticeably larger fruit and thicker, more leathery purple-black skin. Like all jaboticaba, the grape-like fruit erupts directly from the trunk and older branches in dense clusters, and the tree typically produces one large main flush per year rather than the near-continuous cropping seen in 'Sabara'. New foliage emerges an attractive salmon-pink before maturing to deep green, adding ornamental value alongside the fruit. Grow it in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and expect a slow-growing but very long-lived tree that rewards patience with sweet, translucent pulp for fresh eating or preserves.
sources: Purdue University Horticulture — Jaboticabas (Morton, Fruits of Warm Climates)
California Rare Fruit Growers — Jaboticaba Varieties
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Jaboticaba Production in Florida
